metadata.title: How Apple's John Ternus inherited a 'reckoning' with China

content.text:
Strategy Risks founder and CEO, Isaac Stone Fish, sits down with Market Domination host Josh Lipton to discuss various aspects of Apple's (AAPL) overall strategy in China, India, and more.
So you argue in this great new piece, uh Isaac, you say Apple faces what you call is a reckoning that can no longer be avoided or hedged because of the the depth of its integration with China. Just start there. Explain what you mean by that.
Apple for the last several decades made a multi-hundred billion dollar bet on engaging with China, with the Chinese Communist Party, with Chinese supply chains, with Chinese data laws, and with Chinese consumers. And now in 2026, we are very much in a bifurcating world. And companies the world over, but I would argue especially in the United States and China have to start picking sides, have to balance between the US and China. And this is the position that Apple's new CEO finds himself in.
Of course, when we talk about this relationship, I think a lot of investors will immediately go to manufacturing, right? Um now Apple will say, listen, we are diversifying, right? We're going to Vietnam, we're going to India. So what is your push back against that?
Around the margins, sure. but Apple is so incredibly dependent on China, not only because Apple Apple is, but the manufacturers it's using in India, in Vietnam, in Malaysia are also dependent on China and Chinese supply chains. So there's no way for Apple to be removing even even to the degree that we'd like China from the equation without massive, massive changes.
So if if Apple says, you know, if the iPhone says made in India, how much is that product still dependent on China?
I think that if you had to choose, Apple would absolutely need China more than India even if it says made in India. I mean Apple would have to invest probably similar amounts in India that it's invested in China in order to make this work.
Can India ever become the the China for Apple or no?
It's a it's a existential question for India's economy. I hope so, but it's so far not looking great for that.
Can China make it harder for Apple to diverse diversify away from China?
Apple's doing uh China's doing that right now. It's
How do they do that?
They're sometimes quietly, sometimes loudly pushing on manufacturers to prevent them from decoupling from China. They passed a law recently that restricts the ability from companies to decouple from China. There's new sanctions measures that makes it harder. and there's just a lot of phone calls between Chinese executives and Indian executives, Vietnamese executives, Thai executives, reminding them on which side their bread is buttered. and that makes it very, very challenging for Apple to navigate.
So now spin forward. How does our great new AI era further complicate all this?
So it may be a way out for Apple because AI might be more of a software versus a hardware issue. It may be that that Apple can depend on US AI versus Chinese AI or it might be that Apple uses this to integrate Chinese AI into its phones, into its models, becoming the first major US company to do that. And then we see a very different version of a national security risk.
All right, so now, so now let's talk solutions, right? What how should they pivot? You talk about what you call, you use this phrase Isaac in the piece. You say, manage decoupling. What what does that mean and what could that potentially cost Apple?
So Apple's been historically one of the world's most successful companies and what I argue is Apple has to better price its risk. And right now it is too exposed to China, too exposed for the Chinese Communist Party for the geopolitical shifts that we're seeing. And so basically it is on a line by line item and for a company like Apple, there's tens of thousands. Price out the cost of the China engagement, figure out what that is, and then figure out how do you successfully and cost effectively decouple in a way that doesn't jeopardize the work that you're doing in China, so that there's not one major tug but a very, very slow movement.
